::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Heat and surface ozone ($\text{O}_3$) harm the same staple crops, often in the same places and the same weeks, because ozone forms faster in hot weather. Counting them separately misreads both: one global study found that 24%, 9.8% and 46% of the yield loss that statistics attribute to extreme heat in wheat, maize and soybean was really caused by the extra ozone on hot days. Ozone on its own cut global yields in 2010–2012 by an estimated 12.4% for soybean, 7.1% for wheat, 6.1% for maize and 4.4% for rice. Projected to 2050 without adaptation, warming cuts global crop production by 11%; rising ozone makes that 15%, while cutting ozone precursors brings it to 9.0%. Which response helps most depends on the crop: heat-tolerant cultivars for maize and soybean where heat dominates, ozone control for wheat.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Corrected, October 2026

An earlier version of this page said co-occurring heat and ozone cut soybean, wheat and maize yields by $4.4$–$12.4\%$ beyond heat alone. Those figures are ozone-only global yield losses, ranging from rice to soybean, from a study that does not estimate a heat-plus-ozone increment. The page also gave a $5$–$15\%$ global ozone loss, a per-crop loss table, a bar chart and a $15$–$30\%$ fall in photosynthesis that no cited source contains; described ozone's effect on RuBisCO loosely, where the evidence is for less of the enzyme rather than a less active one; and presented a four-tier adaptation plan as the content of a *Frontiers in Climate* editorial that does not discuss it. Its interactive widget used response coefficients from no source and has been removed, as have a data note that named no dataset and a code link to a repository that does not exist. The page now reports what the cited studies find.
:::

## Heat and ozone arrive together

Ozone formation is strongly correlated with temperature, so the hot days that stress a crop also tend to be its high-ozone days[^1]. The two stresses overlap in space as well. A global map of five yield constraints found that areas with high ozone losses are often also at risk of high losses from heat stress, pests and diseases, and to a lesser extent aridity and nutrient stress. In India, the area where ozone cuts wheat production most coincided with the area of highest heat stress, which covered most of the northern half of the country[^2].

Because the two arrive together, a statistical model that relates yields to hot days alone credits heat with damage done by the ozone that came with it. Tai and colleagues measured heat as killing degree days: over the season, the sum of each day's maximum temperature above the crop's optimal growth temperature. They then corrected for the covariation of ozone with temperature and found that, on average, 24% of wheat's, 9.8% of maize's and 46% of soybean's observed yield sensitivity to killing degree days came from the higher ozone associated with hot days. For rice the result was inconclusive[^1].

## What ozone does inside a leaf

1. Ozone enters leaves through the stomata and generates other reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative stress that decreases photosynthesis, growth and biomass[^3].
2. Antioxidants in the water film on the cell walls, ascorbate among them, can detoxify ozone and its products, but they are used up in doing so[^4].
3. The leaf ends up with less RuBisCO, the enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide. A review of about 20 experimental studies found that ozone lowers RuBisCO's concentration rather than its activation state. The fall has been attributed to slower synthesis of the enzyme's messenger RNA, though one study points to faster breakdown[^4].
4. Leaves senesce earlier and faster. In wheat this shortens the time from flowering to maturity, leaving less time to fill the grain, and the yield loss is mostly in the mass of each grain rather than the number of grains[^4].

How much does this cost? Using the ozone dose taken up through the stomata, Mills and colleagues estimated that ozone in 2010–2012 cut global yields by 12.4% for soybean, 7.1% for wheat, 6.1% for maize and 4.4% for rice each year, 227 million tonnes of lost yield in all, and ranked sensitivity soybean > wheat > maize > rice[^2]. These are losses to ozone alone, measured against clean air; they are not an addition to the losses from heat.

## Which staples are most exposed

The two global studies answer different questions, so the columns below are not comparable with one another:

| Crop | Yield lost to ozone, 2010–2012[^2] | Share of apparent heat sensitivity that is ozone[^1] | Main driver of projected 2050 change in major producing regions[^1] |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Soybean | 12.4% | 46% | Temperature in South America; uncertain in the US |
| Wheat | 7.1% | 24% | Ozone, except in South America, where temperature |
| Maize | 6.1% | 9.8% | Temperature in the US, Europe and South America; ozone in China |
| Rice | 4.4% | inconclusive | Ozone in China |

The first column is today's loss to ozone alone. The second says how much of the historical link between hot days and poor harvests was really ozone. The third says which of the two stresses dominates the change projected to 2050 in the regions that grow most of each crop.

## Projected to 2050

Tai and colleagues projected 2000-to-2050 changes in temperature and ozone with the Community Earth System Model under two scenarios: RCP4.5, in which pollution control lowers surface ozone worldwide except in South Asia, and RCP8.5, in which ozone rises worldwide except in the US and Japan. They converted the yield changes of the four crops into food energy and left out the effects of rising carbon dioxide, of adaptation and of water scarcity[^1]:

| Change in global crop production by 2050 | RCP4.5 (ozone falls) | RCP8.5 (ozone rises) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Warming alone | −11% | −11% |
| Ozone alone | +3.1% | −3.6% |
| Both together | −9.0% | −15% |
| Undernourishment in developing countries, 18% in 2000 | up 27%, to about 23% | up 49%, to 27% |

The combined effect is computed grid cell by grid cell and crop by crop, as the product of a climate and an ozone factor, so it is not the sum of the two rows above it. Regionally the range is wider: wheat production in South Asia, where ozone worsens in both scenarios, falls by up to 40%, and maize and soybean in their temperature-dominated regions fall by 20–50% from more frequent extreme heat whatever happens to ozone. The undernourishment rate under RCP4.5 is $18\% \times 1.27 = 22.9\%$.

## What would help

The studies point to three kinds of response, and which one pays depends on whether heat or ozone dominates a crop's losses.

**Cut ozone at its source.** Under RCP4.5, ozone regulation could fully reverse the warming impact on wheat in the US and China and turn it into a gain. Tai and colleagues argue that, given how hard ozone-resistant cultivars are to deploy, the doubtful efficacy of other management practices and the public-health benefit of cleaner air, ozone regulation may be a practical and preferable complement to climate adaptation, depending on the crop, and call for farmers, agricultural policy makers and air-quality managers to work together[^1]. Mills and colleagues likewise list more stringent controls on ozone precursor emissions as one way to close the ozone yield gap[^2].

**Breed for heat and ozone tolerance.** Selecting heat-tolerant cultivars may work for maize and soybean in their major producing regions, except China for both crops and the US for soybean, but less well than ozone reduction for wheat[^1]. Varieties differ widely in ozone tolerance, most of all in soybean and rice, which leaves room to select more tolerant ones, and Mills and colleagues describe a crop ideotype tolerant of several stresses at once, ozone included[^2]. There is a trade-off. Drying soil normally closes stomata, which limits ozone uptake, so drought-adapted varieties that keep their stomata open under drought take a higher ozone dose; yet those are the traits that keep them productive under drought, so breeding against them may not raise yield[^4].

**Manage the crop and its nitrogen.** Mills and colleagues discuss changes in crop management that could reduce ozone impacts in the shorter term[^2]. The *Frontiers in Climate* Research Topic that we edited gathered farm-scale work of this kind[^5]. One study found that optimising fertiliser input could raise maize production by 20–25% without increasing nitrogen losses in regions such as Eastern Europe, Western Africa and parts of Central and Eastern Africa. Another found that of three cover crops, white clover, a living mulch, reduced greenhouse-gas emissions and had the highest potential to mitigate climate change. A third, from Vietnam, found that the main obstacles to adopting climate-smart agriculture were a lack of capital, information, technical support and land-ownership institutions.

## Key takeaways

- Ozone formation rises with temperature, so heat and ozone peak together, and the areas at risk from each overlap. Ignoring ozone credits heat with its damage: 24% of wheat's, 9.8% of maize's and 46% of soybean's apparent sensitivity to extreme heat came from ozone.
- Ozone enters through the stomata and forms reactive oxygen species; the leaf holds less RuBisCO and senesces early, which shortens grain filling. In 2010–2012 ozone alone cut global yields by 12.4% for soybean, 7.1% for wheat, 6.1% for maize and 4.4% for rice.
- Without adaptation, warming cuts global crop production by 11% by 2050; rising ozone makes it 15%, falling ozone 9.0%.
- Heat-tolerant cultivars suit maize and soybean where temperature dominates; ozone control suits wheat. Breeding for ozone tolerance has to weigh drought-adapted traits that keep stomata open.
